root_cause_note: ai.meta.com / llama.com HTTP 400 was NOT Meta blocking. It is a defect in scripts/fetch.py's header set: Meta rejects a Chrome User-Agent that arrives WITHOUT Sec-Fetch-* headers. Adding Sec-Fetch-Mode/Site/Dest (or using a non-Chrome UA) returns 200 on every Meta surface. Separately, fetch.py's Wayback step dies with requests.exceptions.ContentDecodingError on some snapshots (openai.com), which the ladder reports as 'no snapshot'; reading the body with stream=True + raw.read(decode_content=False) recovers it. Both defects caused surfaces to be recorded as unreadable when they are readable. fetch.py also never escalates to Wayback on 400 (RETRY_STATUS lacks 400).

findings.finding: Under a shadow evaluation on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, an agent built on Opus 4.8 (run via the OpenClaw scaffold, six days and thousands of dollars of compute) completed the engineering unaided but produced papers the original authors unambiguously rejected, exhibiting five recurring failure modes.
findings.finding_quote: both papers were unambiguously rejected by the authors
findings.models_systems: Opus 4.8 (Anthropic), run under the OpenClaw scaffold
findings.institution: Princeton University (CRUX Core Team), with UK AI Security Institute, Cornflower Labs, University of Toronto, UC Berkeley, Georgetown CSET, Johns Hopkins, Stanford and others
findings.domain: Agentic AI R&D capability / recursive self-improvement
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes - an empirical model finding measuring agent behaviour. Gate 2 (a) yes and (b) yes (Opus 4.8 named), but (c) fails: this is a capability-shortfall result that the authors themselves read as evidence against explosive progress, i.e. a reassuring null with no dangerous threshold crossed, so no company response is reasonably called for. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: in scope - named external evaluator (Princeton CRUX team), independent of the developer
findings.access_type: external evaluator, API access with own scaffold (OpenClaw)

findings.finding: A robustness re-run of one of the two case studies using GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex, its native scaffold, under matched time and API budgets reproduced nearly all of the same failure modes, indicating the failures are not an artefact of the OpenClaw scaffold.
findings.finding_quote: this run reproduced nearly every single one of our identified failure modes
findings.models_systems: GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex (OpenAI), native scaffold
findings.institution: Princeton University (CRUX Core Team), with UK AI Security Institute and co-authors listed above
findings.domain: Agentic AI R&D capability / evaluation methodology (scaffold sensitivity)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes - an empirical model finding. Gate 2 (a) yes, (b) yes (GPT-5.6 Sol/Codex named), (c) fails: a capability-shortfall replication serving as a methodology robustness check, no dangerous threshold crossed and no concerning behaviour warranting a company response. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.access_type: external evaluator, API access via the developer's own native scaffold (Codex)

items.title: Better answers, broader thinking: What students gain from ChatGPT and critical-thinking training
items.date_source: page byline in the recovered Wayback snapshot 20260828010717 (August 27, 2026)
items.rule_cited: §1 company-venue carve-out - an external evaluator (Bocconi University) is named, so it enters under the evaluator with 'company-published' on Finding Type
items.reason: Randomised experiment with 1,000+ Bocconi first-year undergraduates run by Bocconi researchers with OpenAI Economic Research. The §1 test on a company venue is 'is an external evaluator named?' - it is, so the piece is in scope rather than a company self-report.

findings.finding: In a randomised experiment with more than 1,000 first-year undergraduates assigned to ChatGPT access (GPT-4o), causal-reasoning training, both, or neither, students given ChatGPT access scored almost a full point higher on a five-point human-graded rubric and produced work more similar to expert-written recommendations.
findings.finding_quote: The students who had access to ChatGPT scored almost a full point higher on the five-point scale.
findings.institution: Bocconi University, in collaboration with OpenAI Economic Research
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: what is measured is human student output under an access treatment, not model behaviour. GPT-4o is the instrument/treatment of a human-subjects study, so this is not an empirical model finding. Tier C, Action Trackable blank.
findings.scope: in scope via §1 company-venue carve-out - Bocconi University named as external evaluator
findings.access_type: product access (ChatGPT), external academic evaluator on a company venue

findings.finding: Causal-reasoning training raised the originality and variety of student ideas but produced no gain on the grading rubric, which measured only how well recommendations addressed two marketing goals - a documented measurement-instrument blind spot showing that conventional rubrics can miss originality once AI makes polished output cheap.
findings.finding_quote: Students who completed the exercise explained more clearly why their ideas might work and when they might fail, but did not score higher on the grading rubric
findings.institution: Bocconi University, in collaboration with OpenAI Economic Research
findings.domain: Evaluation methodology / assessment design in education
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails - a methodology finding about the sensitivity of a human grading rubric, not an empirical model finding. Tier C, Action Trackable blank. Retained as a distinct row from the access effect because it is a separate, independently codeable claim about the measuring instrument rather than about the treatment.
findings.access_type: product access (ChatGPT), external academic evaluator on a company venue
